name: Orchid extract

lead: Orchid extract is a botanical from several orchid species, such as Dendrobium and Phalaenopsis, used in Asian skincare. It is marketed as an antioxidant for fresher, younger-looking skin.

The idea is that antioxidants reduce oxidative stress in skin so it looks younger. Published work consists of cell and animal studies plus patents, for example a Phalaenopsis extract in a cell model of sun-induced pigment spots and a patent for Dendrobium chrysotoxum in anti-aging cosmetics. No human skin trial was found.

paras: Used as an ingredient in creams, serums and essences within an anti-aging or brightening routine. Because the term covers different species, products vary in what they contain.
No safety data specific to cosmetic orchid extracts were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Orchid extracts from species such as Dendrobium and Phalaenopsis are used in Asian skincare as antioxidants, aiming at less oxidative skin stress and a fresher, younger look. Published work consists of lab and animal studies and patents.

lead: Orchid extract refers to preparations from various orchid species used in cosmetics, most often marketed as antioxidant, brightening or anti-aging botanicals in Asian skincare. The orchid family (Orchidaceae) is very large, so the term covers different species, such as Dendrobium and Phalaenopsis, with different chemistry.[1]

People use orchid-extract serums and creams with the aim of a brighter, more even and youthful-looking complexion. The proposed routes are antioxidant activity, reduced pigment-cell differentiation and protection of skin cells from ageing stress, all described in laboratory and patent material rather than in human skin trials.[2][3]

Published research is mostly laboratory and animal work. Examples include a Phalaenopsis extract tested in a cell-culture model of sun-induced pigment spots and a Dendrobium extract tested in rats for bone loss.[2][4] Patent filings describe Dendrobium chrysotoxum extract for anti-aging cosmetic use.[3][5] No human clinical trial of an orchid extract for skin appearance was found.

paras: Orchids are one of the largest plant families. Beyond ornamental use, some orchid parts have culinary and perfumery roles: the ground tubers of terrestrial orchids make the drink and ice cream known as salep, and vanilla comes from the seed pods of Vanilla orchids.[1] Cosmetic orchid extracts are a separate category and are typically derived from species such as Dendrobium or Phalaenopsis.

Phalaenopsis (moth orchids) is a genus of about seventy species native to Asia, New Guinea and Australia and among the most popular orchids sold as potted plants.[6] Dendrobium species include Dendrobium officinale, a traditional Chinese medicinal herb widely used in Asia that is reported to have anti-chronic inflammation, anti-obesity and immune-modulating properties,[4] and Dendrobium chrysotoxum, the species in the anti-ageing patent filings.[3] Other orchids studied for traditional uses include Cyrtopodium species, whose extracts have been used as human phytotherapeutics for analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties and for healing skin lesions.[7]

A 2016 study reported that a Phalaenopsis orchid extract inhibited WNT1-induced differentiation of immature melanocyte precursors in a co-culture model designed to mimic solar lentigo (sun spots). The model co-cultured a squamous carcinoma cell line that expresses high WNT1 with normal human melanocytes, because increased WNT1 is reported to accelerate melanocyte stem-cell differentiation in solar lentigines.[2]

A 2012 patent filing describes an anti-aging composition containing Dendrobium chrysotoxum extract, which it says may prevent signs of skin ageing and promote cell or tissue longevity, and describes an extract that inhibits the mitochondrial protein Smac/DIABLO.[3][5] Further patent filings from 2010 and 2011 describe cosmetic or dermatological compositions containing an orchid extract.[8]

A Dendrobium officinale extract prevented bone loss in ovariectomized rats and inhibited osteoclast differentiation in vitro, which concerns osteoporosis rather than skin.[4] A 2020 preprint reported that a Dendrobium officinale extract improved wound healing in diabetic mice, linking this to reduced inflammation and NF-kB signalling.[9] A Cyrtopodium glutiniferum extract was profiled by mass spectrometry and tested in vitro for antiproliferative and genotoxic effects.[7]
No studies found. Related work on orchid extracts is limited to cell-culture and animal studies, as described above, and patent filings.

Orchid extracts are marketed in Asian skincare, where orchid-derived ingredients are used as antioxidant and anti-aging botanicals. Orchids also have culinary and perfumery roles: ground tubers of terrestrial orchids make salep, and vanilla comes from orchid seed pods.[1] Cosmetic marketing claims for orchid extracts are not paired with published human skin trials.
